title: RAII: Attaching Cleanup to the Object Instead of the Code Path

questions.question: When does a destructor run?
options: Automatically, when the object's lifetime ends, on every path out
When you call it explicitly
When the program exits
When the garbage collector decides to
questions.explanation: The compiler emits the call on every exit path, including early returns and exceptions unwinding the stack. That guarantee is what makes the pattern work.

questions.question: Why is a resource handle usually not copyable?
options: Two copies would each release the same resource, and a double release is worse than a leak
Because copying is slow
Because the compiler cannot copy classes with destructors
Because resources are always large
questions.explanation: A double close can shut a descriptor that another part of the program has since opened for something else, producing a bug nowhere near its cause.

questions.question: What does = delete on the copy constructor do?
options: Makes the compiler reject any attempt to copy, at the line that attempts it
Frees the object's memory when it is copied
Marks the constructor as private
Deletes the object after it is copied
questions.explanation: It is enforcement rather than convention, and it reports the problem where the mistake is written rather than where the damage happens.

questions.question: Why does close() set the id to nothing before calling fake_close?
options: So a second call, including the one from the destructor, has nothing left to do
Because fake_close requires it
To make the function faster
Because the id is const
questions.explanation: Marking the handle empty first makes close idempotent, so calling it early and then letting the destructor run cannot release the same device twice.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an example of this pattern in the standard library?
options: std::move
std::vector
std::unique_ptr
std::lock_guard
questions.explanation: std::move is a cast that expresses intent and owns nothing. The other three acquire something in their constructor and release it in their destructor.

questions.question: How does this compare with Python's with statement or C#'s using?
options: Those require the caller to remember the block, RAII puts the guarantee in the type
They are identical in every respect
They are safer because they are explicit
They also run on exceptions, which RAII does not
questions.explanation: A caller who forgets the block gets no cleanup in those languages. With RAII the default behaviour is already correct.
